opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it came from my own experience as a student. When I started at Tsinghua, especially in the computer science courses, there was a lot of information asymmetry. Some students had senior classmates who passed down notes, past exams, or advice on which approaches actually worked for the big programming assignments. Others had nothing and had to figure everything out from scratch, often wasting a lot of time on things that weren't really the point of the course.

So I felt that putting my work out in the open was a simple way to level the playing field. It's not about letting people copy. Honestly, if someone just copies, they're hurting themselves, and the teaching staff can usually tell anyway. The value is in having a reference: seeing how someone structured a project, what kind of code quality is possible, how to write a report, what pitfalls exist. When you're stuck at 2 a.m. on some systems assignment, a working example can teach you a lot.

There's also the open-source mindset. I'd benefited enormously from open-source projects and from people sharing knowledge online for free. Open-sourcing my coursework felt like a small way to give back and contribute to that culture locally, within my own school community.

And selfishly, it pushed me to do better work. If you know other people are going to read your code, you write it more cleanly, you document it, you think more carefully. So it helped me grow too. Later I'd hear from younger students that some of those repos saved them a lot of pain, and that was really rewarding to hear.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly describes information asymmetry among Tsinghua students and says sharing work could level the playing field.

r002.rationale: It says some students lacked notes and advice, but does not identify them as highly capable students.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from my own frustration as a student. When I was doing the coursework at Tsinghua, a lot of the assignments were things people had done many times before, but you couldn't find anything useful about them. You'd hit a wall at two in the morning on some compiler project or an OS lab, and there was nobody to ask, no record of how previous people had gotten through it. Every year, hundreds of students were basically rediscovering the same bugs and the same dead ends from scratch.

That felt wasteful to me. Not the learning part, the struggling-in-the-dark part. So when I finished something I was reasonably proud of, I thought, why not put it on GitHub? If someone next year gets stuck at the same place, they can at least see one way to think about it. Not to copy, but to unblock.

And I think there's a bigger point. In open source generally, you build on what came before. Nobody writes a deep learning framework from zero anymore. But in school, we pretend every student exists in isolation. I didn't believe that was how people actually learn. I learned more from reading other people's code than from any lecture, so I wanted to give that back.

There were concerns, of course, about cheating. But my view was that if an assignment can be defeated by a public repo, the assignment should be better, not the repo hidden. And the students who just copy don't get much anyway. The ones who read it, compare it with their own approach, and figure out why mine was different, those are the ones it actually helps. Later I got messages from people saying it saved them a week, or that it was the first time they understood a concept, and that confirmed for me it was the right call.

r001.rationale: The response describes students lacking useful information or records and says sharing assignments could help later students avoid repeating the same dead ends, communicating reduced information gaps among Tsinghua students.

r002.rationale: It says students struggled to find information, but does not identify them as highly capable.
